title: The ship that was replaced
paras: The puzzle attributed to Plutarch concerns a ship preserved by the Athenians in commemoration of Theseus, whose timbers, as they decayed, were replaced one at a time until, it was said, not a plank of the original remained. Philosophers disagreed whether it was still the same vessel, and Hobbes, characteristically, sharpened the case by supposing that someone had gathered the discarded planks and reassembled them. There are now two rival claimants, one retaining the form and unbroken history of the original, the other retaining its matter. The temptation is to treat the dispute as a factual one awaiting a sufficiently ingenious argument, as though the ship's identity were a hidden property that careful scrutiny might eventually disclose.

That temptation deserves resistance. The word 'same' covers a family of relations which coincide so regularly in daily life that we seldom suspect their plurality. A river retains its identity although no drop of its water persists; a statue melted into a bell leaves the bronze unchanged yet destroys the statue. In the first case we track the form and course of a process, in the second the stuff of which a thing is made, and neither practice is mistaken. Ordinarily the criteria converge and no question arises. The ship is troubling not because it exposes a gap in our knowledge but because it drives the criteria apart and compels us to say which we meant, something our usage never obliged us to decide.

The puzzle acquires more than antiquarian interest when transferred to persons, whose constituent matter is renewed at differing rates, whose memories are reconstituted rather than preserved, and whose characters alter beyond easy recognition over decades. Candidates for what secures personal identity, whether bodily continuity or chains of overlapping memory and psychological connection, can be separated by thought experiments in which a person is duplicated, so that two beings wake with identical recollections. Each criterion yields a verdict in ordinary circumstances; in extraordinary ones they yield rival verdicts, and nothing in our practice tells us which to prefer.

From such cases Derek Parfit drew a radical conclusion: that personal identity is not what matters in survival. What we value, when we hope to survive, is the continued existence of someone psychologically continuous with ourselves, who remembers our life and prosecutes our projects; whether that successor is strictly identical with us may be an empty question, no more determinate than whether a society that disbands and later re-forms is one society or two. Parfit reported this realisation as a release: the boundaries between himself and others seemed thinner, and his own death less alarming.

Critics are not so consoled. If my future self is merely a sufficiently close successor, it becomes difficult to explain why I should feel for that person the peculiar concern I now feel for my own old age, or why I should be held answerable for what a predecessor did decades ago. Parfit's reply, that such concern can survive the loss of its metaphysical foundation, being rooted in connection rather than identity, is ingenious but not obviously sufficient, for it leaves unexplained why degrees of connection should carry the moral weight that identity was supposed to supply. The ship, it seems, carries a heavier cargo than its builders intended.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?

title: Moral luck
paras: Consider two drivers who, after the same convivial evening, make the same imprudent decision to drive home, and who are equally careless at the same bend. On one road a child steps out; on the other, nobody does. The first driver is a killer and the second merely a fortunate offender; the first will be censured, punished and perhaps haunted for life, while the second sleeps untroubled. Our reactions, and the law's, register the difference with confidence. Yet the sole difference between the two lies in something neither driver governed, and this is precisely what a venerable principle of morality forbids us to treat as relevant.

The principle, to which Kant gave its most austere form, holds that moral assessment applies only to what lies within an agent's control. Its intuitive appeal is deep: to blame a person for events that fortune alone determined seems no more defensible than to blame him for his height. But the principle collides with a settled practice of judging agents by what they do and bring about, and what they do and bring about is shaped at every point by contingencies beyond their command. Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, in companion essays of 1976, named the resulting tension moral luck.

Among the varieties Nagel distinguishes are luck in outcomes, as in the case of the drivers; luck in circumstances, since many of the blameless would have disgraced themselves had history tested them, and many of the condemned would have passed unnoticed in gentler times; and luck in constitution, the temperament and dispositions that no one elects. The unsettling feature of such a list is its tendency to expand. Pressed to its limit, the demand for control dissolves the agent into a series of antecedent causes, leaving little for which anyone could be held answerable, so that the principle which was meant to protect responsibility threatens to abolish it.

Two responses are available. The first, rationalist in spirit, holds that the drivers are equally culpable and that our harsher reaction to the first is an error: understandable as the product of grief and of the need to find someone answerable for a death, but indefensible as a judgement of character. The law's distinction between causing death and merely endangering life then appears a concession to sentiment and not a principle. The second response accepts moral luck as a genuine feature of our condition. We are not pure wills hovering above the world, and what we answer for includes the way our deeds turn out.

Williams inclined to the latter, and pointed to agent-regret, the distinctive sentiment of one who has caused harm without fault. The lorry driver who, through no negligence, runs over a child may be assured by everyone that he is blameless; we would nonetheless think less of him if he felt no more than a bystander would. That reaction is not a mistake about blame, since by hypothesis nobody blames him. It indicates, rather, that our relation to our actions cannot be exhausted by the vocabulary of control. Whether this vindicates moral luck, or merely shows that regret and blame are separable, is a question the example cannot settle.

title: Trusting experts
paras: A moment's reflection discloses how little of what we believe we have verified for ourselves. That the earth orbits the sun, that tobacco promotes cancer, that a city I have never visited exists: none of these could I defend by producing the evidence, and in each I rely on testimony, on teachers, textbooks, physicians and the long chain of persons behind them. Philosophers in the empiricist tradition were inclined to regard such reliance as an intellectual concession, tolerable in the child but unworthy of the mature mind, which ought to resolve to believe nothing it has not examined. The ideal is noble; it is also, in the conditions of modern knowledge, unattainable.

No individual could master the evidence for climate science, the safety of vaccines and the structure of the atom, any more than a single artisan could manufacture a computer. The division of cognitive labour is as indispensable to inquiry as the division of manual labour is to industry. Hence the person who disdains experts does not thereby become more rational; he merely exchanges the judgement of identifiable specialists for that of whoever he happens to find congenial, and he does so, as a rule, without registering the exchange. Self-reliance in belief is, for most questions, a fiction, and an expensive one.

Yet it does not follow that trust should be unconditional. The layperson's predicament is that the ordinary method of appraising a claim, scrutinising its evidence, is the very one denied to him, and he must therefore rely on indirect indicators. Has the field a record of predictive success? Is there agreement among specialists who are independent of one another, or merely among those who share an interest? Does the speaker stand to gain from a particular conclusion? Is the claim made within the speaker's competence, or is a physicist pronouncing on monetary policy? These questions demand no technical training, yet they distinguish reasonable trust from credulity.

Indicators of this kind are fallible, because expertise itself fails in patterned ways. Specialists are most dependable on questions resembling those they have often encountered, and least dependable when circumstances change in ways their training did not anticipate; and a discipline can be captured by its own orthodoxies, rewarding conformity and penalising dissent. Healthy institutions anticipate these defects with peer review, replication, the publication of data and the shielding of awkward critics, devices which, notably, work by making experts answerable to one another and not to the public at large.

The appropriate attitude is thus neither deference nor suspicion but something more exacting: calibrated trust, proportioned to such evidence of reliability as a non-specialist can actually observe. It is harder to practise than either extreme, which may explain why both remain popular. To follow neither, a layperson must do the unglamorous work of asking, of each claim, who is speaking, to whom the speaker answers, and what he would lose by being wrong.

title: Why projects run late
paras: Invited to forecast the duration of a task, people characteristically err on the side of brevity. Students underestimate the time their dissertations will consume, householders the expense of renovation, and governments the cost of bridges and railways, sometimes by multiples. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky christened the tendency the planning fallacy: the disposition to predict that one's own undertakings will fare better than comparable undertakings have fared in the past. In one study, students asked when they would finish their theses predicted an average about three weeks shorter than the one they eventually took, and even their 'worst case' forecasts proved too sanguine. What makes the phenomenon remarkable is not that people are ignorant of that past, but that they hold the relevant knowledge and fail to apply it.

The explanation lies in how predictions are generated. A student who has finished every essay late will nonetheless forecast that the next will be done early, yet will judge a classmate's prospects far more soberly. Contemplating our own task, we construct a narrative of the steps required, in which each step proceeds more or less as designed. We seldom incorporate the illness, the missing file or the unexpected demand that disrupted every prior attempt, because each of those disruptions was a different surprise, and the aggregate of unforeseeable surprises is never itself foreseen. Kahneman termed this the inside view, in which a case is considered in all its particularity.

The outside view disregards particulars and asks a plainer question: how long have projects of this kind, taken together, actually required? A builder estimating a kitchen refit does better to consult the durations of the last twenty than to itemise the tasks of this one. The outside view feels less informative because it discards what is distinctive about the case; it is generally more accurate for the same reason, since what is distinctive is precisely what we are most inclined to overweight.

Cognitive optimism is not the sole mechanism. Within organisations a realistic estimate may kill a project before it begins, so that those who favour it have reasons to present the sanguine version, and once money has been committed even a failing venture is hard to abandon. The planning fallacy has, accordingly, an institutional counterpart, in which errors of individual judgement are reinforced by the incentives of the people around them, and in which the person who forecasts honestly is penalised for doing so.

Remedies exist, though none is popular. Reference-class forecasting, which builds the outside view into formal budgets, has been adopted by some governments for large infrastructure; and the premortem, in which a team imagines that the project has already failed and reconstructs the reasons, surfaces risks that its members would rather not mention. The simplest counsel remains the hardest to follow: when your plan says three weeks, consult how long the last plan took.

title: Remembering as rebuilding
paras: We are inclined to picture memory as a recording: an experience is deposited in the brain and, when we recall it, replayed, perhaps somewhat faded. A century of research has rendered this picture difficult to defend. Remembering appears to resemble the reconstruction of a scene from fragments far more than the playing of a tape, the lacunae being filled by general knowledge, expectation and even the phrasing of the questions we are asked.

Frederic Bartlett demonstrated as much in the 1930s by asking students to retell an unfamiliar folk tale at intervals. With each repetition the story grew shorter, more coherent and more like the narratives the students already knew; unfamiliar details were omitted or transmuted into familiar ones. Subsequent work by Elizabeth Loftus and her collaborators showed that a single verb could shift recall. Subjects who watched a film of a collision and were asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other offered higher estimates, and were likelier to report broken glass that had not been present, than subjects asked about cars that 'hit' each other.

Even vivid memories enjoy no exemption. After shocking public events, researchers have asked people where they were when they heard the news, and have asked them again a year or two later. The accounts frequently diverge substantially while the confidence of the rememberers remains high: students who had written down their recollections of the Challenger disaster the morning after, and were asked again two and a half years later, often produced a different story and were certain that the later version was the true one. The sense of vividness, it appears, is a poor guide to fidelity, and the confidence with which a memory is held cannot be treated as evidence of its truth. Nor need we suppose that such witnesses lie; the more disquieting inference is that they sincerely report what they have come to believe.

The implications for law are considerable, since eyewitness testimony has long been regarded as powerful evidence. Many convictions later overturned by DNA analysis had rested on confident but mistaken identification, and researchers have proposed reforms to the conduct of line-ups and to the questioning of witnesses, so that the procedure does not itself supply the details which the witness subsequently remembers.

It would nonetheless be an error to conclude that memory is simply defective. A system that preserved every detail would be costly and, arguably, less useful, since the retention of everything is not the same as the capacity to use anything. Reconstruction allows us to generalise from experience, to imagine the future with the same machinery we use to recall the past, and to make sense of events in place of merely retaining them. The price of this flexibility is that memory serves the present at least as much as it records the past.

title: Choosing without knowing why
paras: In a study published in 2005, researchers showed volunteers pairs of photographs of faces and asked them to select the more attractive in each pair. After every choice the experimenter slid the chosen card across the table and invited the volunteer to explain the preference. On some trials, by a simple sleight of hand, the volunteer was handed instead the face that had been rejected. Most of the time nobody noticed, although the faces lay side by side and the volunteers could look as long as they liked. More striking still, volunteers went on to justify a preference for a face they had not chosen, sometimes citing features, such as earrings, which only the rejected face possessed.

The manipulation was, in short, mundane; what was extraordinary was the ease with which it passed unobserved. The investigators named the phenomenon choice blindness and have since found it in other settings. Shoppers asked to sample two jams or two teas failed to notice when the samples had been covertly exchanged before they explained their preferences; the jars were fitted with two compartments, so that a quiet inversion accomplished the swap. In a survey on political questions, respondents whose answers had been reversed on the page defended positions they had just rejected, and some later shifted their stated views toward the reversed answers.

These results are congenial to an older argument in psychology, that people have less access to the causes of their own behaviour than they suppose. In the 1970s Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson had shown that subjects readily gave confident reasons for behaviour which experiments traced to quite different causes. Their subjects, asked to choose the best of four identical pairs of stockings laid in a row, favoured the pair on the right, yet cited the texture and sheen of the stockings and never the position. Asked why we chose something, we may be reporting not a reason that drove the choice but a plausible story composed after the fact. The story feels like memory, and we possess no inner signal that distinguishes inventing from recalling.

It would be rash to conclude that stated reasons are worthless. Detection rates rise substantially when the swapped options differ markedly, or when people care a great deal about the decision. Choice blindness demonstrates that our sense of knowing our own minds is fallible, not that it is invariably mistaken. Its practical lesson may be modest but is worth heeding: surveys, interviews and even our own diaries record what people say about their choices, which is not the same thing as why they made them. Where a stated reason cannot be checked against anything else, it is better treated as a datum to be explained than as an explanation to be accepted.

title: Is willpower a muscle?
paras: In an experiment of the late 1990s, hungry volunteers were seated in a room redolent of freshly baked cookies. Some were permitted to eat the cookies; others were obliged to eat radishes and to leave the cookies untouched. All were then set a puzzle which, unknown to them, could not be solved. Those who had resisted the cookies abandoned the puzzle markedly sooner. The effect was large and the design easily copied, and the experimenters proposed that self-control draws upon a limited resource, depleted by one act of restraint and therefore diminished for the next. For two decades the result was cited in textbooks, in policy papers and in the advice offered to dieters.

The hypothesis, soon christened ego depletion, owed much of its appeal to its fit with ordinary experience: after a day of onerous decisions the biscuit tin is harder to resist. Hundreds of studies seemed to corroborate it, and some investigators went further, proposing that the depleted resource was glucose and that a sugared drink might restore flagging willpower. Popular books counselled readers to schedule difficult choices for the morning and to regard willpower as a muscle that tires with use. The theory was elegant in a further respect: it promised a single mechanism for dieting, drinking, temper and procrastination, and this power to unify such disparate failures lent it an authority that no individual study could have earned.

Doubts grew as psychology began to scrutinise its own methods. Small samples, flexible analysis and a preference for publishing positive results can jointly generate a literature replete with effects that are not really there. In 2016 a consortium of more than twenty laboratories ran the same carefully specified depletion task and found an effect close to zero; the laboratories had agreed the protocol and registered their plan before collecting any data, which left no scope for flexible analysis. Even the meta-analyses that had seemed to confirm the effect proved to be distorted by selective publication, and correcting for it reduced the estimated effect sharply. The glucose explanation fared no better, since critics observed that the brain's consumption of sugar barely alters during demanding mental work.

The tale is not simply one of a theory overturned. Later large studies have yielded mixed results, and some researchers contend that the tasks employed were too feeble to deplete anyone. Others have found that people who believe willpower to be limited exhibit depletion-like effects, while those who do not show little. If so, fatigue after effort may be real but shaped by expectation and not by a fuel gauge in the brain. What the episode incontestably shows is how a finding that seems to explain everyday life may spread far beyond the strength of its evidence.

title: Can we harm people who do not exist yet?
paras: We commonly suppose that the unborn can be wronged. A government that entombs radioactive waste in a manner certain to breach containment in three centuries seems to act wickedly towards those who will then be living, although not one of them is alive to be injured today. Our legislation, our pension schemes and our conservation efforts all presuppose that those who come after us have claims upon us, and the presupposition seems too natural to need defence. A great deal of what we believe we owe the future depends upon intuitions of this kind, and it is therefore disquieting that Derek Parfit, in the 1980s, showed them to rest on a foundation far less secure than they appear.

The argument begins from an unglamorous fact about reproduction. Which person is born depends upon the precise moment of conception, and this in turn depends on innumerable circumstances in the lives of the parents: had yours met a year later, or conceived a month later, someone else would have been born in your place. A far-reaching policy, such as a choice between consuming a resource swiftly and husbanding it, alters how millions work, travel and encounter one another. Within a few generations the individuals who exist under one policy will be wholly different from those who would have existed under the other; the two futures may share a population in number, but not in persons.

Suppose, then, that we select rapid depletion, and that people two centuries hence enjoy a lower, though still worthwhile, quality of life than their counterparts would have enjoyed under conservation. Have we harmed them? On the ordinary understanding of harm, as making someone worse off than he would otherwise have been, it seems we have not. Had we chosen conservation, these particular people would never have existed, and since their lives are worth living, our choice has made none of them worse off. The conclusion is perverse, for the choice still seems wrong; yet its wrongness cannot be located in a victim.

Parfit called this the non-identity problem, and he inferred that our moral thinking cannot rest wholly on the interests of particular persons. What matters, he proposed, is the quality of the lives that will be led, whoever the persons living them turn out to be. The inference is not forced upon us: some philosophers have defended person-affecting accounts, and others have questioned whether bringing someone into a worse life can be harmless merely because the alternative was non-existence. But the difficulty is practical as well as academic. In debates about climate policy, where decisions taken now will determine both how future people live and which people there will be, the argument that posterity cannot complain, since it owes its very existence to our choices, is a position someone could seriously advance, and one which an adequate ethics must be able to answer.

title: Can a lobster suffer?
paras: Until recently the animal-welfare statutes of many jurisdictions protected only vertebrates. Crabs, lobsters and octopuses lay beyond their reach, which is why a lobster might lawfully be boiled alive where the same treatment of a chicken would be a crime. The boundary was drawn less by evidence than by habit, and by the intractable difficulty of ascertaining what, if anything, such creatures feel. It is worth observing that the difficulty is of a peculiar kind: it arises not from a missing instrument but from the absence of any agreed test.

Because we cannot interrogate a crab, and because behaviour resembling distress may be a reflex with nothing felt behind it, investigators have looked for converging indirect indicators. Does the animal guard an injured part of its body? Will it weigh avoidance of harm against competing needs? Hermit crabs subjected to mild shocks within their shells, for instance, abandoned poor shells more readily than good ones, as though trading the discomfort against the value of the dwelling. Does it learn to shun places where it was hurt, and will it seek relief when injured? No single indicator establishes feeling; their conjunction renders it more or less probable. The method is that of the clinic or the courtroom, not the laboratory bench: a verdict is reached on the balance of probabilities, by weighing evidence none of which is individually decisive.

In 2021 a team at the London School of Economics, led by the philosopher Jonathan Birch, reviewed more than three hundred studies against such criteria, and judged the evidence of sentience sufficiently strong in cephalopod molluscs, and in decapod crustaceans such as crabs and lobsters, to warrant legal protection. The following year Britain extended its welfare legislation to both groups. The report advised against boiling decapods alive, but it did not pretend to certainty: it urged further research, and it presented its conclusions as a judgement about what the evidence made reasonable and not as a proof.

The episode models a form of reasoning under uncertainty with a range well beyond lobsters. We shall probably never know what it is like, if it is like anything, to be a crab. But the question for law is not whether we are certain; it is how strong the evidence must be before reasonable care is owed. Where the cost of precaution is small, as in stunning an animal before killing it, and the cost of error is great suffering, the demand for proof that may never arrive is itself a decision, and not obviously the cautious one. To insist on certainty before extending care is to assign the entire risk of our ignorance to the creature least able to bear it. The costs of a false positive and a false negative are unequal, and a policy that ignores the inequality is not thereby neutral.

title: The number you heard first
paras: In a celebrated experiment of the 1970s, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune before their volunteers. It had been rigged to stop at either 10 or 65, and the volunteers, who watched it turn, knew that it bore no relation to what followed. They were asked whether the proportion of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than the number the wheel had shown, and then to estimate the true figure. Those who had seen 10 gave a median estimate of 25 per cent; those who had seen 65 gave 45. A number known to be random had drawn their judgement toward itself.

The effect, termed anchoring, has since been found far from the laboratory. Experienced estate agents shown different asking prices for the same house valued it differently, while insisting that the figure had not influenced them. German judges of long standing, who rolled loaded dice before recommending a sentence for a shoplifter, proposed longer terms after high throws. Retailers exploit the same tendency in printing a crossed-out 'original' price beside a reduced one, and in negotiation the first offer tends to shape the final settlement. In each case the anchor is conspicuous, or arbitrary, or both, and in each case those affected deny being affected, which is perhaps the most instructive feature of the phenomenon.

Two explanations have been proposed, and both may be correct. On the first, people begin from the anchor and adjust away from it, but halt prematurely, as soon as they reach a value that seems plausible. On the second, the anchor quietly summons information consistent with itself: contemplating a high price makes a house's merits more vivid, and a low price its defects. Either account would explain why the effect persists even when people know the anchor to be irrelevant. The two are not merely academic rivals, for they suggest different remedies: the first implies that people might be induced to adjust further, whereas the second implies that the damage is done at the moment the anchor is encountered, so that urging further adjustment would achieve little.

Anchoring is notably robust. Even absurd anchors, such as asking whether Gandhi died before or after the age of 140, can nudge subsequent estimates, and people with genuine expertise are seldom immune, though they are sometimes less affected. Warnings help only a little. The most reliable remedy appears to be deliberate consideration of the opposite: asking why the anchor might be mistaken and generating reasons for a very different answer. Nor is the effect confined to the kind of numerical judgement that a laboratory can conveniently measure; it appears wherever a quantity must be guessed and a convenient reference point lies to hand. It is easier recommended than practised, since the whole difficulty is that an anchor does its work without our noticing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?

options.t: Anchoring affects only the judgements of novices, and can be eliminated entirely by warning people that an irrelevant number is present.
options.why: Paragraph 4 says experts are seldom immune and that warnings help only a little.

options.why: Too narrow, and it merges the two explanations, which the passage treats as separate.

options.why: Experts are seldom immune.

options.t: Starting from the first plausible figure that comes to mind and adjusting until the result seems reasonable.

options.t: Warning people about the anchor before they judge will remove its effect entirely, whatever the task.
options.why: Contradicted: warnings help only a little, and the second explanation implies the effect arises at once.

options.t: Experts will be wholly unaffected by anchors, because they are able to recall far more relevant information.
options.why: Paragraph 4 says experts are seldom immune.

options.t: Urging people to adjust further from an anchor will do little to reduce its effect.
options.why: The paragraph says that on the second explanation the damage is done when the anchor is encountered.

options.t: The effect will disappear whenever the anchor is plainly seen to be random by those who judge.
options.why: The wheel of fortune shows that a plainly random anchor still works.

recall.q: What median estimates were given by volunteers who had seen the wheel stop at 10 and at 65?
options: 25 per cent and 45 per cent, respectively.
10 per cent and 65 per cent, respectively.
45 per cent and 25 per cent, respectively.
35 per cent in both groups.

recall.q: What does the author identify as the most reliable remedy for anchoring?
options: Warning people that the anchor is irrelevant.
Deliberately considering reasons for a very different answer.
Asking experienced professionals to make the estimate.
Letting people adjust for as long as they wish.

summary.model: A first number, even an irrelevant one, pulls later estimates toward it, often unnoticed; considering the opposite seems to help more than warnings.

title: What the marshmallow test measured
paras: In the late 1960s and early 1970s the psychologist Walter Mischel offered preschool children at a Stanford nursery a choice: they might eat one treat, such as a marshmallow, at once, or wait alone in a room for up to twenty minutes and receive two. The experiment's attraction lay in its austerity, a single child, a single sweet and a closed door. Years later Mischel and his colleagues followed up some of the children and reported that those who had waited longer went on to do better at school and to cope more effectively with stress in adolescence. The test became a famous emblem of self-control and of the notion that the capacity to defer gratification in early childhood predicts success in later life.

The original follow-ups, however, involved small numbers of children, almost all from families connected with the university. In 2018 a team repeated the study with a larger and more varied group of nearly a thousand children. Waiting longer was again associated with later achievement, but the association was about half as strong as before, and it shrank much further once the researchers allowed for the children's family background, home environment and early cognitive abilities. Much of what the test appeared to predict, it seemed, had already been captured by those other factors. A sample so narrow as the original could scarcely have distinguished the influence of a child's temperament from the influence of the child's household.

A different line of inquiry questioned what waiting means. In a 2013 experiment, children first dealt with an adult who either kept or broke a promise to supply better art materials. Those whose adult had proved unreliable waited, on average, only a few minutes for the second marshmallow, while those whose adult had been dependable waited several times as long. The researchers inferred that the decision to wait is in part a judgement about the environment. For a child whose experience has taught that promises are often broken, taking the sweet at once is not a failure of willpower but a rational wager.

None of this shows that self-control is unimportant, or that Mischel's research was worthless; he himself warned against treating the test as a measure of fixed character. But the history of the marshmallow test illustrates how a vivid experiment may carry a message larger than its evidence. Read one way, it suggested that some children are simply born with more discipline. Read in the light of later findings, it suggests that the capacity to wait depends heavily on whether waiting has ever paid off, a reading with the further merit of being actionable, since it directs attention to the conditions in which children grow up and not to the dispositions with which they are said to begin.

options.why: Paragraph 2 says the association remained, though weaker.

options.why: Paragraph 3 argues that such children are making a rational judgement, not showing a lack of self-control.

options.t: Mischel's original findings were distorted, and his conclusions should therefore be set aside by psychologists as unsound.
options.why: Paragraph 4 says his research was not worthless and that he warned against the popular reading.

questions.stem: Compared with the original follow-ups, the 2018 study:

options.t: found no association at all between waiting and later achievement in the larger and more varied group.
options.why: The association remained, at about half its former strength.

options.t: found a stronger association among children from less advantaged homes than among the more favoured.
options.why: No such subgroup result is reported.

options.t: found a weaker association, which shrank further once family background and early abilities were allowed for.
options.why: Paragraph 2.

options.t: found a similar association, which persisted undiminished once background was considered by the researchers.
options.why: Half right: the association was weaker and shrank further with controls.

options.t: lacking the capacity for self-control that other children possess.
options.why: The experiment's point is that this is not a failure of willpower.

options.t: acting sensibly, given experience that promises are often broken.
options.why: Paragraph 3 calls it a rational wager for such a child.

options.t: less intelligent than the children who are able to wait.
options.why: Intelligence is not discussed in the experiment.

options.t: displaying a trait of character that will persist throughout later life.
options.why: The author warns against treating the test as a measure of fixed character.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, the author's attitude to Mischel's work is best described as:

options.t: respectful, while critical of the way in which the test was popularly interpreted.
options.why: He is said not to be worthless and to have warned against the popular reading; the message 'larger than its evidence' is the criticism.

options.t: dismissive of his methods while admiring of his conclusions.
options.why: Reversed: the conclusions are qualified, and the work is not dismissed.

options.t: defensive, since the later studies have unfairly diminished his reputation.
options.why: The author treats the later studies as informative, not unfair.

options.t: neutral, since the author merely reports the history of the experiment without assessing it.
options.why: The paragraph assesses the experiment, notably its message larger than the evidence.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most support the view in the third paragraph that waiting reflects a judgement about the environment?

options.t: Children whose earlier rewards had arrived as promised waited longer for a second marshmallow elsewhere than other children.
options.why: Past experience of reliable reward changes how long a child waits, which is the environmental judgement described.

options.t: Children with larger vocabularies waited longer than children with smaller vocabularies, and their families were no better off.
options.why: Vocabulary is unrelated to the environmental explanation.

options.t: Children who could not wait at the age of four were also less patient at the age of fourteen.
options.why: Consistent with a fixed trait, and so it does not support the environmental reading.

options.t: Children tested alone waited longer than children tested in pairs, which suggests that company shortens patience.
options.why: Testing conditions of this sort are not the reliability of promises.

recall.q: What did the 2013 experiment vary?
options: The length of time the children were left alone.
Whether the adult kept or broke a promise before the test.
The kind of treat offered to each child.
The age of the children who took part.

recall.q: How did the 2018 sample differ from the original one?
options: It was larger and more varied, with nearly a thousand children.
It was smaller but drawn from a single university.
It consisted only of children from poorer families.
It was followed for a shorter period of time.

summary.model: The marshmallow test's link to later success shrank in larger studies; waiting reflects children's circumstances as much as fixed self-control, though self-control still matters.
